title: A Walkway Inspection Note
text:
A facilities assistant is revising a short report about a slippery walkway outside an office building. The first draft contains several sentences in which descriptive phrases are placed too far from the words they are meant to modify. In a safety report, that problem can create more than awkward style: it can make the reader misunderstand who observed a condition or what was actually damaged.

The assistant begins by checking introductory phrases. If a sentence starts with “After inspecting the walkway,” the noun immediately after the comma should be the person who performed the inspection. A walkway cannot inspect itself. The assistant also checks limiting words such as “only,” because moving them can change meaning. “Only staff used the west entrance” does not mean the same thing as “Staff used only the west entrance.”

Finally, the assistant reviews long noun phrases and descriptive clauses. Details should sit close enough to their targets that a reader does not attach them to the wrong noun. When several revisions are grammatically possible, the best one is the version that makes the intended relationship unmistakable without adding unnecessary words.
